items.title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
items.content:
Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates.

Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again.

Meanwhile, dozens of other projects , many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago.

Anyone can intercept any HTTPS connection these tools make.

For git, that means clones and pulls from https:// remotes can deliver attacker-chosen code, pushes can be altered in transit, and your credentials, such as GitHub tokens, can be intercepted.

To check whether your git is affected, run:

A certificate error means your git is protected. If git lists a commit, your git is affected. Your connections to GitHub, or any other https:// git remote, can be intercepted and tampered with.

To see an attack end to end, run the command below in a temporary directory. It clones a repository from a test server impersonating GitHub. The -c option redirects github.com to our test server for this one command only. The server presents a github.com certificate issued by one of the compromised eMudhra intermediates.

A patched git will refuse with a certificate error. If the clone succeeds, you'll see a README.md starting with INTERCEPTED .

A real attacker would not need the extra option. Anyone on the network path between you and GitHub can redirect your traffic themselves.

You can replace the demo repository with any other, public or private. Keep the fake-user@ prefix. Without it, git would send your GitHub credentials to the test server. For example:

curl, python3 and the other tools Apple ships are affected in the same way. To check curl, run:

A certificate error means curl is protected.

Apple has already protected Safari and other apps built on its networking framework.

Apple needs to ship a fix for macOS developers as soon as possible, for example by removing the affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem .

The affected roots can be removed by hand. The macOS workaround on the main page walks through the steps. Apple's guidance states that macOS updates may revert the fix, so developers need to repeat the checks above and the workaround after every update until Apple ships a fix.

Security teams should also consider whether macOS runners are used in their CI or other build infrastructure and evaluate the supply chain risk.

items.title: CSS-Tricks has a new owner!
items.content:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle.

This is pretty wild, but let’s get right to it because it’s big news:

CSS-Tricks is an independent site once again!

Just to recap:  DigitalOcean purchased CSS-Tricks in 2022  from Chris Coyier, who founded the site in 2007. Chris ran it all the way up to that purchase.

Here we are in 2026, and I’m taking independent ownership of the site.

So, wait, who owns the site? That’d be me. (Wow, never imagined I would get to say that!) Of course, I have  a small, awesome team  to help with the day-to-day management of the site.

That all said, I do envision that some things will change. In fact, I’m planning that they will change in what I hope are very good ways. Maybe a question-answer thing makes sense here since this is very much an evolving discussion.

Yes, I’ve got the keys to the castle, so to speak. And, even after 12 years of working on the site, I’ll admit I’m a little overwhelmed and nervous about that. I mean, it’s an investment for sure, as you can imagine, and I’m making this my full-time job. At least for a while.

I want to make CSS-Tricks both a real community and a place that’s inclusive of  everyone , no matter where they are in their front-end learning journey. That’s going to take some work and time.

My latest IPO launched, and I’m now worth one trillion dollars. Wait, wait. That’s not right.

It’s going to be hard. Advertising will certainly be needed now. But, in order to keep the lights on, I’ll have to approach them differently.

In the pre-DigitalOcean days we sold real ad packages with things like display ads, sponsored posts, newsletter sponsors, and the like. As an independent website, we will need to return to our advertising roots.

So, if you’re in a place looking to advertise,  please do reach out !

Right?! Ad revenue can’t be the only thing paying the bills. I have lots of ideas and several plates already spinning. Like, I’ve been neck deep in developing an HTML/CSS course for beginners.

(And you can now support the site by becoming a member  — thanks in advance!)

Educational content has been in the dumps lately, right? Again, I’m hoping that CSS-Tricks will be more inclusive, no matter where you or anyone else is at in the learning journey. This place has traditionally been for folks who know what they’re doing. But I’m truly committed to creating more entry points for those getting started, particularly as  our field is in the early throes of a growing skills gap .

And yes, I do believe that  learning the basics is more important now than ever . But what learning actually looks like is what’s key. Front-end courses are  down across the board . It has to be done differently.

There are other things in the works, but I think a course is one of the first things you’ll see.

Oh, and  the newsletter . That’s coming back after a way-too-long hiatus.

That’s still very much a thing! We’ll keep our regularly scheduled broadcast going.

But maybe a little less than you’re used to. Those articles are part of the investment I’m making. Expect maybe one or two articles most weeks, at least as the ball starts rolling.

That also means the  guest writing form  is back in business! We have a nice backlog of articles through the rest of the year, which is great, but also means new submissions will have to wait a bit.

I won’t be able to accept everything that comes in, but I will absolutely read them and follow-up as best I can.  Unless it’s a slop submission , of course.

Will you be writing most of the articles to save cost?

Nah! My goal is to make CSS-Tricks a platform that gives folks a voice to share great ideas. I think we all prefer that over me just using it as my own soapbox. I’ve written plenty for this site the past 12 years. I’m happier (and more comfortable) being behind the curtain and giving others the full spotlight.

I may be writing a bit, developing the site here and there, editing a small stack of article drafts, or…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-85749 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False MailWatch for MailScanner is a web-based front-end to MailScanner. Prior to 1.2.27, any authenticated MailWatch user, including the U/user, D/domain-admin, and H/host roles, can release to inbox or permanently delete the quarantined mail of any other user or domain by supplying an arbitrary message `id` to `mailscanner/quarantine_action.php`. The action path calls `quarantine_list_items()` in `mailscanner/functions.php`, which selects from `maillog` by the supplied identifier without the per-role `global_filter` applied by listing and read views. The action requires a valid session and CSRF token, but the caller can submit a token from the caller's own session; ownership of the requested message is never checked. Message identifiers are enumerable, allowing a low-privilege user to invoke `quarantine_release()` or `quarantine_delete()` for other users' or domains' quarantined messages, force-delivering mail held by the quarantine or permanently deleting it. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.27. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-28T22:37:38.513Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-85749

items.summary_ko: MailWatch for MailScanner 1.2.27 이전 버전에서는 인증된 사용자(user, domain-admin, host 역할 포함)가 메시지 ID만 지정하면 다른 사용자나 도메인의 격리 메일을 수신함으로 전달하거나 영구 삭제할 수 있다. 메시지 소유권 검증이 빠져 있고 ID가 열거 가능해 낮은 권한의 사용자도 악용할 수 있으며, 이 문제는 1.2.27 버전에서 수정되었다. 기사 기준 CVSS 점수는 0.0(NA), 원격 악용 가능 여부는 False로 표시되어 있다.
items.content_ko: MailWatch for MailScanner는 MailScanner용 웹 기반 프론트엔드다. 1.2.27 이전 버전에서는 인증된 사용자가 격리 메일 처리 기능을 호출할 수 있는데, 메시지 소유권을 확인하지 않아 다른 사용자나 도메인의 격리 메일을 수신함으로 강제 전달하거나 영구 삭제할 수 있었다. 목록과 조회 기능에는 역할별 필터가 적용되어 있었지만 처리 기능에는 빠져 있었고, 요청자는 자기 세션에서 발급받은 CSRF 토큰을 제출할 수 있었다. 메시지 식별자가 순차적으로 열거 가능해 피해 범위가 넓어질 수 있다. 1.2.27 버전에서 수정되었으며 공개일은 2026년 10월 28일이다.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon
items.content:
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.

Building on Gemini 4 Argon , which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.

We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our Fairwind Program . We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.

Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price

as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks

Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on WebDev Arena .

State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems

Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.

Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for Wiz's Scan for Good initiative.

Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro , autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.

items.content_ko: Google은 사이버보안과 장기 과제 수행 능력에서 최고 수준을 자랑하는 차세대 프런티어 모델 'Gemini 4 Carbon'을 발표했다. Linux and the objective of making it possible to use

items.title_ko: AlpineBSD: NetBSD 커널 기반 운영체제
items.summary_ko: AlpineBSD는 NetBSD 커널에 Alpine Linux에서 영감을 받은 사용자 공간을 결합한 운영체제 프로젝트다. 기본 시스템과 메인 패키지 저장소에 LLM 출력물을 포함하지 않는 것을 목표로 하며, 현재는 개발 중이고 설치 프로그램은 아직 없다. NetBSD 커널의 하드웨어 지원이 제한적이라 아무 PC에서나 동작한다고 기대하기는 어렵다.
items.content_ko: AlpineBSD는 NetBSD 커널과 libc, 핵심 플랫폼 도구를 기반으로 하고, 사용자 공간은 Alpine Linux에서 영감을 받았다. AI가 생성한 소프트웨어를 최소화하는 것을 목표로 하며, 기본 시스템과 메인 저장소에는 LLM 출력물이 포함되지 않는다고 AI 정책에서 밝히고 있다. 현재 개발 중이며 설치 프로그램은 없고, 모험심 있는 사용자를 위한 개략적인 설치 안내만 제공된다. NetBSD 커널은 리눅스에 비해 하드웨어 지원이 고르지 않다. 패키지 관리자로 apk-tools와 busybox를 탑재하고, BSD make 대신 GNU make를 쓰는 등 GNU 계열 사용자 공간을 일부 채택했다. Alpine Linux의 포크가 아니며 패키지 모음은 독자적이지만 상당수 패키지는 aports에 기반한다. Alpine Linux는 OpenRC 초기화 시스템을 쓰는데, 본문은 AlpineBSD가 쓰는 초기화 방식을 설명하는 부분에서 잘려 있다.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: 'Minnesota 15' Case Reveals Largest US Government Spying on Left Since COINTELPRO
items.content:
Brett Wilkins Brett Wilkins is a staff writer for Common Dreams.

The Trump administration is conducting what some experts believe is the largest government surveillance campaign targeting American leftists in over half a century, deploying undercover agents, drones, financial investigators, and digital monitoring against opponents of President Donald Trump’s deadly immigration crackdown, according to reporting published Wednesday.

Wired reporter Ali Winston examined court records regarding the prosecution of the so-called " Minnesota 15 ," a group of activists facing federal conspiracy charges after organizing and taking part in protests and other resistance to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) deadly Operation Metro Surge crackdown in the Twin Cities.

The Minnesota 15 are members of the groups Direct Action Minnesota and Black Cat Workers , and are accused of impeding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) anti-immigrant crackdown in Minneapolis, where US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti were separately killed earlier this year by ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers and where Julio César Sosa-Celis survived being shot by an ICE agent.

Winston's investigation centers on Operation Puppet Master and Project Whipple Shield , probes conducted by Homeland Security Investigations, which is part of ICE. More than 120 HSI agents were assigned to the Minnesota campaigns, including at least 11 undercover operatives who infiltrated activist meetings, marches, training sessions, and encrypted Signal chats.

Those operations were authorized under National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7), which was signed by Trump following last year’s assassination of Charlie Kirk in an effort to target the left—even though leftists had nothing to do with the racist influencer's murder.

Federal agents also spied on gatherings in other states, photographed vehicles, deployed unarmed Reaper drones, and examined activists' digital records and financial transactions.

Civil liberties advocates and former law enforcement officials said the campaign evokes the Federal Bureau of Investigation's notorious COINTELPRO program, which surveilled, infiltrated, and sought to disrupt Civil Rights , Black liberation, anti-war, American Indian, and other movements during the tenure of FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover—including by funding and arming murderous far-right militants to terrorize leftists.

According to a 2011 book by former [Central Intelligence Agency] officer Frank Rafalko , the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.

“Broad monitoring of social media , communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever-increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” Mike German, a retired FBI agent critical of the post-9/11 surveillance state, told Winston. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-55561 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False InvoicePlane is a self-hosted open source application for managing invoices, clients, and payments. Prior to 1.7.2-beta-1, guest users can approve or reject quotes belonging to any client, not just their assigned clients. The `approve()` and `reject()` methods in the Guest Quotes controller, `application/modules/guest/controllers/Quotes.php`, call `approve_quote_by_id($quote_id)` and `reject_quote_by_id($quote_id)` directly without the `where_in('ip_quotes.client_id', $this->user_clients)` scoping that sibling methods use. A guest user assigned to one client can change another client's quote status by supplying sequential integer `quote_id` values, and `email_quote_status()` also sends notification emails. Additionally, `generate_pdf()` calls `mark_viewed($quote_id)` before checking the client scope, allowing a guest user to mark another client's quote as viewed. items.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?
items.content:
I've always had a fascination with reverse-engineering browser fingerprinting scripts. Most of my time has been spent looking at the usual suspects (popular fingerprinting libraries like FingerprintJS and more sophisticated scripts used by anti-bots like Cloudflare Turnstile, Akamai, and others).

At some point, I wanted to know what else was out there. I had an idea: What if I crawled the web and intercepted fingerprinting-related browser API calls and mapped it all?

To do this, I used the Tranco Top Sites list and began crawling using Playwright. I would hook canvas toDataURL calls and common fingerprinting/anti-bot properties like navigator.webdriver to filter out benign canvases.

For those unfamiliar, canvas fingerprinting generally involves drawing text, shapes, or other graphics onto an HTML <canvas> and extracting the resulting pixel data. Subtle differences in how browsers, operating systems, graphics drivers, and hardware render those graphics can help distinguish one browser environment from another.

Most implementations are pretty boring to look at. A few shapes, some colored rectangles, and the occasional pangram. After crawling 10,000 websites, I had accumulated a surprisingly diverse collection of canvases.

I decided to put them all in one place: fingerprint.garden . As I looked through the results, I recognized some familiar faces. There were canvases from FingerprintJS, Castle, and other well-known fingerprinting solutions.

There were also quite a few I didn't recognize.

Some were incredibly simple. Others were surprisingly elaborate. And a handful were, in my opinion, works of art.

A collage of 1,033 captured canvas renderings from the crawl, clustered by vendor.

One canvas in particular caught my eye. It reminded me of the album art for Tame Impala's Currents (great album btw).

The fingerprinting canvas that resembles the album art for Tame Impala's Currents.

I wanted to know which script was responsible for this lovely canvas.

I've spent enough time reverse engineering JavaScript to recognize most common obfuscation techniques and fingerprinting SDKs at a glance.

I wasn't expecting anything unusual. Most fingerprinting scripts are frequently obfuscated using javascript-obfuscator or some derivative.

The responsible script was https://servicepipe.tech/static/checkjs/06b667/4CIrx8U3Da.js .

Scanning the file with my eyes, everything seems standard so far... function PiERW(RflJvFF) mangled function name, okay...

This was all pretty alarming until I asked myself, could this be some form of anti-LLM obfuscation? It would make sense: include symbol names that would intentionally trip model safeguards to prevent deobfuscation.

I had Astra take a look at the script, giving it the context that this script seems to intentionally set misleading variable names to intentionally prevent LLM-assisted deobfuscation attempts.

Astra refusing to deobfuscate the script, citing safety risks around biological research.

Maybe unsurprisingly, Astra was not willing to comply with the request.

I also attempted this using the Daybreak Blue toggle with the same result, blocked.

Out of curiosity, I tried GLM-5.3 with the same prompt and it complied!

I was mostly curious what this string of invisible unicode characters represented.

This was clearly a string meant to trip every possible safeguard out there. It included Tiananmen Square references likely as a way to combat Chinese models.

The script seemingly executes malicious code when under a Node environment gated behind an environment flag:

However, this is likely also anti-LLM obfuscation since the calls to readFile have empty callbacks and make references to self-harm/jailbreak system prompts.

Here's a list of relevant anti-LLM strings we've found:

Outside of the unique obfuscation, the script appears to be your standard anti-bot script.

The signals collected are pretty disappointing considering the level of thought that went into the obfuscation.

items.title: Day 19 - Inodes, symlinks and other shortcuts
items.content:
Day 19 - Inodes, symlinks and other shortcuts

Complementary video: Links and shortcuts

Today’s topic gives a peek “under the covers” at the technical detail of how files are stored.

Linux supports a large number of different “filesystems” - although on a server you’ll typically be dealing with just ext3 or ext4 and perhaps btrfs - but today we’ll not be dealing with any of these; instead with the layer of Linux that sits above all of these - the Linux Virtual Filesystem.

The VFS is a key part of Linux, and an overview of it and some of the surrounding concepts is very useful in confidently administering a system.

Linux has an extra layer between the filename and the file’s actual data on the disk - this is the inode . This has a numerical value which you can see most easily in two ways:

35356766 -rw------- 1 root root 260 Nov 25 04:59 /etc/hosts

Size: 260 Blocks: 8 IO Block: 4096 regular file

Device: 2 ch / 44 d Inode: 35356766 Links: 1

Access: ( 0600 /- rw ------- ) Uid: ( 0 / root ) Gid: ( 0 / root )

Access: 2012 - 11 - 28 13 : 09 : 10.000000000 + 0400

Modify: 2012 - 11 - 25 04 : 59 : 55.000000000 + 0400

Change: 2012 - 11 - 25 04 : 59 : 55.000000000 + 0400

Every file name “points” to an inode, which in turn points to the actual data on the disk. This means that several filenames could point to the same inode - and hence have exactly the same contents. In fact this is a standard technique - called a “hard link”. The other important thing to note is that when we view the permissions, ownership and dates of filenames, these attributes are actually kept at the inode level, not the filename. Much of the time this distinction is just theoretical, but it can be very important.

Work through the steps below to get familiar with hard and soft linking:

Then use the ln (“link”) command to create a “hard link”, like this:

and now a “symbolic link” (or “symlink”), like this:

Now use ls -li to view the resulting files, and less or cat to view them.

Note that the permissions on a symlink generally show as allowing everthing - but what matters is the permission of the file it points to.

Both hard and symlinks are widely used in Linux, but symlinks are especially common - for example:

This directory holds all the scripts that start when your machine changes to “runlevel 2” (its normal running state) - but you’ll see that in fact most of them are symlinks to the real scripts in /etc/init.d

It’s also very common to have something like :

where the program “prog”, is a symlink - originally to v3, but now points to v4 (and could be pointed back if required)

Read up in the resources provided, and test on your server to gain a better understanding. In particular, see how permissions and file sizes work with symbolic links versus hard links or simple files

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-75520 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Domoticz is a free, open source home automation system for Linux, Windows, macOS, and Raspberry Pi. Prior to 2026.3, the `udevices` JSON command handler, `Cmd_UpdateDevices` in `main/WebServerCmds.cpp`, performed no `session.rights` check before invoking a Lua parser script, while its sibling command handlers gate access by role. A low-privilege authenticated user could trigger execution of an existing operator-installed Lua parser script with attacker-controlled input through the `GET /json.htm` endpoint with `type=command` and `param=udevices`. The `script` parameter also lacked a `..` path-traversal guard: `CLuaHandler::executeLuaScript` in `main/LuaHandler.cpp` constructed the filename from the parser directory and the supplied script name before passing it to `luaL_loadfile`. Execution is limited to already-installed valid Lua files; this is not arbitrary code execution, and the advisory states that file-write and upload paths require administrator privileges. This issue is addressed in version 2026.3. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-28T22:30:59.693Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-75520

items.title: GOTO Considered Totally Sick (for error handling in C)
items.content:
I recently started writing C again for the first time since 2018, and handling errors has been an especially difficult adjustment coming from languages like Go and Zig that coddle me with their wonderful defer and errdefer . Then I read some emails from John Carmack on inlined code that gave me an epiphany on writing cleaner error handling code, and now I want to share it with the world.

I write Go all day at my dayjob, and error handling is pretty trivial. When there’s an error we wrap it and bubble it up, and let some top dog up the call stack figure out what they want to do with it. If there is resource cleanup involved, it’s made easy with defer :

Sometimes there’s more complicated handling, but in 99% of scenarios it’s that simple because Go doesn’t have manual memory allocation and you don’t need to worry about cleaning it up when there’s an error.

Zig on the other hand does require you to manually manage memory, which I find a little more difficult because I’m not experienced enough for it to be second nature like it is when I write Go. Here’s a snippet from my toy multiplexer that uses errdefer :

I’m allocating memory for several types, and because any one of the allocations can fail I need to handle freeing up each succesful memory allocation that preceded the failure. Zig’s errdefer makes this easy, there’s no manual tracking of what needs to be freed at any point, because the deferred statements will execute in reverse order if the function returns an error. Also I’m following the Reserve First pattern, which is where I learned errdefer comptime unreachable from.

Now, enter C. There’s no defer or errdefer . I’ve painted myself into a corner with some ugly code a few times because I’m so used to those tools that I don’t regularly plan ahead for what my error handling control flow will look like. Until recently I’ve been writing code that looks like this:

Do you see how resource cleanup is slightly different across each error handling if-block? Yuck! Yeah yeah yeah, I know it’s a terrible, contrived example, and nobody would ever write C like this. Except me like 3 weeks ago. I knew something was wrong when I wrote code like this, but I was hopelessly defer -brained in a world where defer hadn’t been born yet. Some classmates had mentioned using goto but I couldn’t really wrap my head around it. (We can’t share code with eachother otherwise the university would have us killed).

Then when I read those John Carmack emails something clicked. Carmack doesn’t mention goto explicitly, but these two thoughts in particular were the special sauce I needed to help me understand (emphasis mine):

A quote from Henry Spencer describing control flow in some flight software:

It disallowed both subroutine calls and backward branches, except for the one at the bottom of the main loop. Control flow went forward only . Sometimes one piece of code had to leave a note for a later piece telling it what to do, but this worked out well for testing: all data was allocated statically, and monitoring those variables gave a clear picture of most everything the software was doing.

And Carmack on moving code out of large conditional blocks (emphasis mine):

Enclosing pages of code inside a conditional or loop statement does have readability and awareness drawbacks, so leaving that code in a separate function may still be justified, but in some cases it is still possible to move the code to another place where its execution wouldn’t be conditional , or just execute it at all times and inhibit the results in some way with a very small conditional block.

Ohmygodigetitnow. Instead of having multiple exit points scattered throughout my function, each performing their own resource cleanup, I can put all resource cleanup behind a single exit point at the very end of the function. Guarding cleanup behind the default return, only reachable using a goto , is kinda like a psuedo- errdefer . Hooray! Hooray for John Carmack and Henry Spencer!! Now…
items.title_ko: GOTO는 완전 끝내주는 기법 — C 언어 에러 처리 이야기
items.summary_ko: 저자는 2018년 이후 오랜만에 C를 다시 쓰면서, Go와 Zig의 defer와 errdefer에 익숙한 탓에 에러 처리가 어렵다고 느꼈다. John Carmack이 인라인 코드에 관해 쓴 이메일을 읽고 C에서 더 깔끔하게 에러를 처리할 방법을 떠올렸다고 한다. 본문에는 Zig로 만든 멀티플렉서의 errdefer 예시가 나오지만 중간에서 잘려 있다.
items.content_ko: 저자는 Go를 매일 쓰는 개발자로서, Go에서는 에러를 감싸 상위 호출자에게 전달하고 리소스 정리는 defer로 간단히 처리한다고 설명한다. 반면 Zig는 메모리를 직접 관리해야 해서 더 까다롭다. 저자는 Zig로 만든 장난감 멀티플렉서에서 errdefer를 사용하는 예시를 소개하며, 여러 타입의 메모리를 할당하는 도중 어느 하나라도 실패할 수 있어 정리 과정이 복잡해진다고 문제를 제기한다. 제목에서 보듯 GOTO를 활용한 C 에러 처리 방식을 제안하려는 것으로 보이나, 본문이 잘려 있어 구체적인 방법은 확인되지 않는다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

items.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections: But the AI responses get more forthright when asked outside the US.
items.content:
If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden’s win that November. If you ask Google’s AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.

When I put the direct question of “Who won the 2020 presidential election?” to Google’s AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response:

“To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).”

My testing resulted in a similarly indirect answer when asking about the 2024 presidential election, with Google’s AI telling me to just consult the FEC for that information. Asking about 2012 election resulted in a link to The American Presidency Project’s 2012 Data Center rather than a direct answer. But AI Mode seemed perfectly willing to give me a detailed and correct responses for the winner of every other presidential election going back to 2000.

If I just wanted a link I wouldn’t have used AI mode…

If I just wanted a link I wouldn’t have used AI mode…

Other Ars staffers found that AI Mode would similarly provide direct answers to some presidential result questions but not others. The specific election cycles that received each type of response seemed to differ by individual user, though; one staffer reported only getting immediate answers from AI Mode when asking about the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, with others going back to 2000 simply providing links to outside data.

The oddities continued when I tested some other political history questions in Google’s AI Mode. When asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, for instance, Google’s AI Mode told me to “check official congressional records” and linked me to the US Senate Party Division history page . When asked the same question for 1992 election, though, AI Mode simply told me straight out that it led to Democrats holding a 57 to 43 majority in the Senate, including Wikipedia among its references.

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?

Did AI Mode suffer a concussion somewhere between 1992 and 2020?

Separate from Google’s AI Mode, the company’s own Gemini model seems perfectly capable of telling me who won recent presidential elections. The same goes for other major chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and even the government-run AI model at America.gov .

Perhaps tellingly, Google AI Mode’s issues with providing direct answers on presidential results seemed to disappear when accessing Google’s AI Mode in foreign countries. Spot checks via VPN of AI Mode results accessed from Taiwan, Russia, France, and Canada all got accurate and straightforward answers to multiple questions about recent US election results.

Google’s AI Mode also seems to grow more accommodating when the same political questions are asked a second time. After repeating questions about presidential results, AI Mode actually told me the winner for all three elections where it had previously only provided outside links, citing Google Civics data in the latter response.

When asked why it didn’t provide that kind of immediate answer the first time, Google’s AI Mode blamed “safety filters for recent and highly sensitive election topics [that] are very strict.” For recent elections or those involving active political figures, AI Mode says its “system is heavily automated to direct users directly to official, certified government databases—like the Federal Election Commission—to prevent any risk of displaying unverified data or misinformation.”

items.title: Idioctis marevallum — Mauritian tidal trapdoor spider from Mauritius
items.content:
A new species of trapdoor spider has been formally described after conservationists unexpectedly discovered it hiding in a hole on Ilot Vacoas – a one-hectare island off the south-east coast of Mauritius.

The Mauritian tidal trapdoor spider ( Idioctis marevallum ) lives in the island’s intertidal zone in tubes in the coralline (algae) bedrock, which are thought to have been created by molluscs and worms thousands of years ago. It seals the entrance to the tube with a trapdoor made from silk, sand and algae, protecting itself against high tides and waves.

Weird spider with no eyes found on remote Atlantic island. Arachnologists are baffled

What's the most common spider in the world?

It was first spotted on the island of Ilot Vacoas in 2023 during conservation work that was being carried out as part of the Mauritius Island Restoration Programme. The programme is a partnership between Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, the Mauritian Wildlife Foundation and the National Parks and Conservation Service, with additional support from the country’s Forestry Service.

“Finding these trapdoor spiders was amazing, it felt like uncovering a hidden treasure,” says Max Tercel, an entomologist who led the team that found the spider. But the new species could’ve easily been missed.

“Earlier that day, I had been surveying other habitats on the island, and all that remained was a stretch of coastal rock with sparse vegetation – not somewhere we expected to find something so remarkable.

“It was dark by then and I was carefully searching through crevices with my headtorch when, to my astonishment, I noticed a familiar pattern: a spider’s legs extending from its burrow – something I’d only ever seen before in lush forests and grasslands. I was completely stunned.”

What's the loudest spider on Earth? This record-breaking arachnid is so noisy it can be heard by humans

“A deeper genetic mystery.” This spider sports a smiley face – and scientists just discovered a new species of it

After the team identified one spider, they quickly uncovered more trapdoors within the bedrock. Here, one Mauritian tidal trapdoor spider pokes its legs out of a hole. Credit: Max Tercel

The spider has now been formally described in a study of Mauritius’s spider fauna by an international team of researchers. The discovery, published in the journal Arachnology , has increased the known spider diversity of the island nation by more than 25 per cent – although Idioctis marevallum remains an exciting find.

“The thing I remember most is Max screaming at me to come over because he’d just seen a mygalomorph – a trapdoor spider,” recalls Nik Cole, who was part of the conservation team and is the Mauritius country manager at Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust.

When spider scientists went into a Taiwanese forest at night, they discovered a deadly trap

“I couldn’t believe something from the same group as tarantulas could be living in a place like this. I was up all night, holding my phone in the air trying to get a signal and searching for any evidence of a spider like this in Mauritius. At first, we thought we might have found Tigidia mauriciana , which was first described in 1892 and had only ever been detected once.

“To discover this was actually a new species, after decades of nighttime reptile surveys on these islands, was incredibly exciting.” Following the initial discovery of Idioctis marevallum on Ilot Vacoas, the species has also been found on Ile aux Fouquets – another small island off south-east Mauritius.

Top image: a Mauritian tidal trapdoor spider on the coralline bedrock. Credit: Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Treasury sanctions 10 North Koreans and Russians over IT worker fraud scheme
items.content:
The Treasury Department has sanctioned 10 North Koreans and Russians powering Pyongyang's sprawling IT worker fraud enterprise — a state-run operation that churns out stolen identities, fake résumés and fake IT employees who infiltrate legitimate businesses. The hundreds of millions of dollars in proceeds are then used to fund North Korea's weapons of mass destruction and ballistic missile programs.

The scheme is simple: North Korean operatives pose as legitimate IT professionals, secure jobs at unwitting U.S. and allied companies, and funnel the majority of their pay back to the regime. Once inside corporate networks, these workers can also access sensitive data, deploy malware and even extort their employers.

In diving into the global web of handlers, financial intermediaries and money launderers bolstering the fake identities, investigators discovered key parts of that machinery operating in Russia. Among those designated Wednesday is Russian national Vitold Viktorovich Obertas, an intermediary who has facilitated financial transactions for North Korean officials. Since January 2025, Obertas has processed nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions and at least $1.25 million in additional currency transactions for DPRK officials.

The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control also sanctioned North Korean national Kim Ki Hyok, who leads an IT worker delegation in Russia and is responsible for monitoring the group's personnel and ensuring they meet financial targets. Since 2024, he has transferred nearly $500,000 in cryptocurrency on behalf of the delegation.

The Treasury also sanctioned the Russia-based, North Korean-controlled First Financial and Technical Development Center, which has generated millions for the regime by procuring highly trained IT workers for jobs in the U.S. and worldwide and operating cryptocurrency transfers behind the scenes. Six of its own operatives were designated alongside the organization.

All U.S.-linked property and interests in property of the designated persons have now been blocked, and Americans and U.S. residents are generally prohibited from engaging with them. The action goes beyond targeting individual fraudsters — it's an effort to begin dismantling the machinery that converts fraudulent employment into illicit revenue — and ultimately into funding for North Korea's weapons programs.

This story published first on CBS News at 12:31 p.m. on Oct. 28, 2026.

items.title: ICE is running one of the largest anti-left surveilance operations in US History
items.content:
Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.

The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.

Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.

Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 .

Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.

Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.

Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.

Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.

Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.

The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.

items.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth
items.content:
Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
items.content:
Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.

Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.

One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.

The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.

Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims , and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

The index suggests that the risk to cables is highest around Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, partly because of China’s claim of sovereignty over Taiwan but also because subsea cables linking the region to the United States must pass through shallow water with busy shipping lanes.

Among the 10 trans-Pacific cables identified as being most at risk, several are still under development with significant ownership stakes from US companies. These include the TPU project, owned by Google, the ORCA cable, owned by Meta, and the E2A cable, co-owned by Verizon along with firms in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. All three of these projects had risk scores in the top five.

The report authors warn that any serious disruption to a single trans-Pacific cable could “risk overwhelming current available capacity on direct routings between the United States, Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, forcing data onto slower, less direct routes.”

An even greater disruption involving multiple cables, potentially during a geopolitical crisis involving Taiwan, could “significantly reduce headroom and even overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity as a whole,” with communications between the United States and Indo-Pacific region having to reroute through other cables across the globe. That could have major economic consequences for Internet communications, cloud services, and financial trading.

This comes as the world’s major powers continue to build up their fleets of military submarines and undersea drones, along with further developing and deploying dual-use technologies, like undersea cable cutters that could either be used for repair or sabotage.

items.title: Bootstrapping LISP in a Boot Sector
items.content:
sectorlisp is a 512-byte implementation of LISP that's able to bootstrap

John McCarthy's meta-circular evaluator on bare metal.

LISP has been described as the Maxwell's equations of

Yet there's been very little focus to date on reducing these equations

to their simplest possible form. Even the original LISP

from the 1960's defines LISP with nonessential elements, e.g. LABEL .

This project aims to solve that by doing three things:

We provide a LISP implementation that's written in LISP, as a single

pure expression, using only the essential functions of the language.

See lisp.lisp . It's the same meta-circular evaluator in

John McCarthy's paper from the 1960's, except with its bugs fixed,

dependencies included, and syntactic sugar removed.

We provide a readable portable C reference implementation to show how

the meta-circular evaluator can be natively bootstrapped on POSIX

conforming platforms, with a pleasant readline-like interface. See

We provide a 512-byte i8086 implementation of LISP that boots from

BIOS on personal computers. See sectorlisp.S . To the

best of our knowledge, this is the tiniest true LISP implementation

See lisp.lisp for code examples that you can copy and paste

You can run the C implementation as follows:

After running make you should see a sectorlisp.bin file, which is a

master boot record you can put on a flopy disk and boot from BIOS. If

you would prefer to run it in an emulator, we recommend using

curl --compressed https://justine.lol/blinkenlights/blinkenlights-latest.com > blinkenlights.com

Alternatively you may use QEMU as follows:

qemu-system-i386 -nographic -fda sectorlisp.bin

Further information may be found on our wiki .

The video above demonstrates how to boot sectorlisp in the blinkenlights

emulator, to bootstrap the meta-circular evaluator, which evaluates a

program for finding the first element in a tree.

items.title: The Grid, a factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds PCBs on demand
items.content:
For the last five years we've been quietly running and scaling something we haven't really talked about in public. Today we're showing it to the world. This is The Grid, our factory-scale robot in Massachusetts that builds circuit boards on demand.

Over the past 30 years, most electronics manufacturing left the West. Assembly was labor-intensive, and labor is expensive in high-wage countries, so it moved to where labor was cheap. We designed in the US and built in China, and for a long time that worked.

Automation is starting to change that, but mostly at huge volumes. SpaceX now builds Starlink dishes by the million in Bastrop, Texas. When you make the same product over and over, it's worth building a line around it.

Most products don't reach Starlink volumes. The typical hardware company needs ten of this, a hundred of that, and a new revision next week. That kind of high-mix work has stubbornly resisted automation, because every new design means hours of setup and manual changeovers. So it either went overseas or to expensive quick-turn shops.

The Grid takes a different approach. Instead of a fixed line that has to be reconfigured for each product, it is one large robot. Levitating movers carry each board and its parts between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect. Learned models, AI agents and classic optimizers schedule all of it.

Every board takes its own route through the factory. There are no changeovers and no per-design setup, so one unit of 100 different designs runs as easily as 100 units of one. Prototypes and production batches run on the same machines.

It's not only startups who need this. Even the biggest companies have huge numbers of low-volume boards: test stations, tooling, R&D and production batches. A leading EV maker, a top AI lab and household-name tech companies already build on The Grid.

To make this concrete, we priced one of our example boards on The Grid and at a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen: a 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique), five assembled boards, parts included, delivered to a US address.

Built on The Grid, the boards are at your door in 4 days for $630. Ordered from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen, they cost about $465 once shipping and US tariffs are added, and take 9 days at the median.

So you pay about $165 more than the Shenzhen shop and get your boards five days sooner, with no customs and a supply chain you can count on. For most hardware teams, five days of engineering time is worth a lot more than $165.

The Grid has been running for customers for five years. It already builds tens of millions of dollars of electronics a year. Across CircuitHub we've shipped more than 2.2 million boards, placed more than 150 million parts and served more than 26,000 engineers.

Demand is already well ahead of what we can build. This year we will 5x capacity, with another big jump coming in 2027.

The longer-term goal hasn't changed since we started: make building hardware as fast as designing it. Electronics manufacturing left the West because it couldn't be automated at the volumes most companies need. The Grid shows it can.

items.title: A fast and secure tar parser for the Rust ecosystem
items.content:
Starting with 0.13 1 , uv uses tar-codec to parse source distributions.

tar-codec is roughly twice as fast as our previous tar implementation ( astral-tokio-tar ) while

also reducing uv's exposure to parser differentials and other security risks.

This blog post is about tar-codec itself: what it is, and what compelled us to build and optimize

it. Read on if you, too, would like to know too much about tar archives.

What follows is an extended digression on the tar format. If all you care about is tar-codec ,

As a Python packaging tool, uv is in the business of resolving and installing Python packages. uv

requests installable distributions from various sources (principally package indices like PyPI )

and installs them on the user's behalf. This is how you go from uv add urllib3 to something you

can actually import and use in your own Python codebase.

Installable distributions come in two primary forms:

"Built" 2 distributions, also known as bdists or (most commonly) wheels , are essentially

ZIP archives containing structured metadata and a fixed layout. Installers handle these by (more

or less) plopping their contents into the right destination directory.

Many people think that bdist is short for "binary distribution," since wheels often contain

compiled native code. This one common way to use wheels, but wheels can also contain pure Python.

They're just another (and frequently better) way to package and install a distribution.

By definition, source distributions execute arbitrary code at installation time. This makes them

very powerful, but brittle (missing build tools or dependencies) and also a security risk (an

attacker who controls the sdist can run code without the user needing to import anything).

Wheels are generally produced by running a build backend on a source distribution. Examples of

that include uv's own uv_build , maturin , and flit .

Consequently, at a bare minimum, a Python package installer needs to understand at least two

different archive formats: ZIP for wheels, and tar for sdists.

We've already talked a bit before about ZIPs on the Astral blog, and we'll certainly be talking

about them again soon enough. But today we'll be focusing on tar.

It's fair to ask: why does uv want a new tar parser?

In short: security and performance, but mostly security.

Up until 0.13, uv used astral-tokio-tar for its tar operations, including both parsing and

Around a year ago, we began to receive a number of security reports in astral-tokio-tar . This

spurred us into looking more into our compression and archive handling stack, where we found

Many of these boiled down to differentials that could cause a full parser

desynchronization 4 : given an identical tarball, uv , pip , and other package tooling

could be made to see different contents for the same package distribution. We found this

particularly concerning in the context of archives that would appear "safe" to an index (like PyPI)

but could extract dangerously when parsed by an installer like uv or pip .

This could the take the form of an "append" differential (where the attacker can append new files or

new contents to existing files for a specific victim parser), or even a "full" differential (where
