items.title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
items.content:
LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years. As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)

Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom. It does not appear to be a 2-in-1 convertible design, though; all the footage was of people reaching up to touch the screen in a normal laptop configuration.

The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared. The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.

Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences. First, it’s much lighter. Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.

Second, the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by the small black cutout that Apple calls the Dynamic Island. Presumably it works similarly to the one we’ve seen on the iPhone, expanding or contracting to show live activities and other information.

Finally, there’s a retro throwback: The Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like the logo on MacBooks of yore.

In terms of specs, this refresh includes the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips—the same ones in the previous refresh. The M6 series has already arrived in other Macs, but it seems Apple is skipping them for this refresh; there were previously reports that Apple planned to hold off on updating the chip until the M7 series, which could have significant improvements for AI performance, just like the recently released A20 Pro chip for the iPhone does.

Memory configurations top out where they did in previous MacBook Pro models with M5 Max: up to 128GB of RAM. That said, storage can now go up to 16TB—if you can afford it.

Preorders start today, and the device will reach consumers on November 6. As expected, the price is the catch. The M5 Pro-equipped 14-inch model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. But if you want the M5 Max, you’re looking at a $4,499 starting point for the 14-inch, and $4,799 for the 16-inch—and that’s not accounting for any potential RAM or storage upgrades.

items.title: Paludohadros proudlovii — new iguanodontian dinosaur from Surrey, UK
items.content:
A partial dinosaur skeleton discovered at a brickworks in Surrey in 2001 has been identified as a previously unknown genus and species of early-diverging hadrosauroid iguanodontian. Named Paludohadros proudlovii , the herbivorous dinosaur lived in the wetlands of what is now southern England about 125 million years ago, during the Early Cretaceous.

Reconstruction of Paludohadros proudlovii in life, with the large predatory dinosaur Baryonyx walkeri in the distance. Image credit: Guilherme Gehr.

The new species belonged to Iguanodontia, a group of herbivorous dinosaurs known for the thumb spikes on many of its members. It is the first iguanodont dinosaur to be formally named after the geological formation in which it was found: the Weald Clay Formation at Smokejacks Brickworks.

“Iguanodontia was one of the first dinosaur groups to be named and is one of the most diverse and widespread ornithischian groups, with fossils dating from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Cretaceous,” said lead author Dr. Ricardo Sakamoto of the Natural History Museum and the University of São Paulo, together with students and colleagues.

“This includes the first ornithischian genus to be named, Iguanodon . In 2021, Iguanodontia was defined as the smallest clade containing Dryosaurus altus , Iguanodon bernissartensis , Rhabdodon priscus and Tenontosaurus tilletti .”

“While the diversity of this clade was relatively low during the Jurassic, recent descriptions and reinterpretations suggest that it was more diverse than previously thought.”

Paludohadros proudlovii was about 5 metres long and weighed an estimated 1.5 to 2 tonnes, making it approximately the size of a rhinoceros. Because its bones had not yet fully matured, the specimen was probably a juvenile that could have grown to roughly twice that size.

“ Paludohadros proudlovii is the first species I’ve ever named, and it’s an honour to work on it,” Sakamoto said.

“I still remember that amazing moment when I realised this was a new species that no one had seen before.”

“ Paludohadros proudlovii was discovered just 100 metres (328 feet) away from Baryonyx remains, which are also held at the Natural History Museum,” said lead author Professor Susannah Maidment, a palaeontologist at the Natural History Museum and the University of Birmingham.

“Although Baryonyx is best known for eating fish, the dinosaur’s last meal also included a baby iguanodontian.”

“We can’t know for sure which species the baby belonged to, so perhaps Baryonyx scavenged the bodies of young Paludohadros proudlovii , or even hunted them when it had the opportunity.”

A paper describing the discovery has been published in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology .

Ricardo J. Sakamoto et al. 2026. A new species of iguanodont dinosaur discovered in the Weald Clay Formation (Early Cretaceous) at Smokejacks Brickworks in southern England. Journal of Systematic Palaeontology 24(2). doi: 10.1080/14772019.2026.2726221

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Emacs Turns 50
items.content:
Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn’t write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world’s first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards.

A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer’s memory—making it among the first “stored-program” machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code.

By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a “line editor” to type their code on teletypes—large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They’d type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display.

One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used.

EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-­sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system.

EMACS’s roots begin with the TECO text editor (originally the “Tape Editor and Corrector”) that Dan Murphy ’65 created in 1962 for the pioneering PDP-1 computer at MIT. The program’s commands were uppercase letters: A user would type “I” to insert text, “D” to delete a character, and so on. When tape gave way as a storage medium to files on a huge shared disk, the “T” in “TECO” came to stand for “Text.” And as years passed, TECO became a full language that programmers could use to create new commands, called macros, for editing their code.

In the fall of 1971, Carl Mikkelsen ’76 created Control-R, an add-on program for TECO that took advantage of “glass teletype” terminals with video displays. Control-R immediately displayed changes to the file being edited on screen; the programmer no longer needed to reprint each line to see the changes. The drawback: The display could show only a few lines of code at a time.

“Experienced and sophisticated users found EMACS to be eminently more usable than any of the previous forms of editing.”

Then, in 1976, Richard M. Stallman, a researcher at the MIT AI Lab, saw a full-screen editor—called E—on a visit to Stanford’s AI Lab. Inspired, he returned to MIT and set out to improve Control-R. The most important change to the program’s underlying structure: Every key ran its own macro when pressed, making Control-R far easier to customize. The lab’s hackers took to Stallman’s code with gusto and started changing and adding commands.

That created an issue for Guy Steele Jr., SM ’77, PhD ’80. A graduate student in the lab, Steele frequently needed to help other lab members debug their programs. “I noticed that it was much harder for me to help someone who was using one of these packages rather than straight TECO,” he recalls. “Eventually, it occurred to me to try [to] broker consensus on a standard set of Control-R commands that everyone could agree to use.”

David Moon ’75, another member of the lab, helped out. Stallman jumped in as well, and eventually he took over. Together, the group assigned a standard set of commands that made use of the Meta key found on many of the lab’s early keyboards: Meta-F would move the cursor forward a word, Meta-B would move it back a word, and so on. items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing 'significant risks' | TechCrunch
items.content:

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post .

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.

The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

items.title: A faster way to compute signed 64-bit floor division by constants
items.content:
Signed integer floor division is where you do a/b and get a result that rounds towards − ∞ ,

whereas standard ( “truncated” ) signed division rounds towards 0 .

As stated in Hacker's Delight: “[I suspect that] floor division more often gives the result you want” .

This article is about floor division where the divisor is known at compile time .

Despite the usefulness of this function, the world of integer floor division is in shambles:

This blog post aims to not only shine light on the fast algorithms, but will also introduce a new fast approach which, with ideal compilation:

The benchmark section has a detailed overview showing per-divisor results over many platforms, for throughput and latency.

It works in all bit-widths, and may find use on some 32-bit or SIMD applications, but the biggest benefit is in 64-bit.

It also can be used for faster positive-modulus, and faster "Euclidean" division (differs to floor division for negative divisors) .

Floor division can be much faster than you probably realise.

Below is a snapshot throughput benchmark for division by 86400 (the number of seconds in one day) , the kind of performance you can expect using most languages' built-in methods, vs fast alternatives outlined in this blog.

items.summary_ko: 부호 있는 정수의 floor 나눗셈은 결과를 음의 무한대 방향으로 내림하며, 0 방향으로 버리는 일반 나눗셈과 다릅니다. 이 글은 제수가 컴파일 시점에 알려진 경우를 다루며, 모든 비트 폭에서 동작하고 특히 64비트에서 이점이 큰 새로운 고속 기법을 소개합니다. 하루의 초 수인 86400으로 나누는 경우를 예로 든 벤치마크도 함께 제시합니다.
items.content_ko: 부호 있는 정수의 floor 나눗셈은 결과를 음의 무한대 방향으로 내림하며, 표준(잘라내기) 부호 있는 나눗셈은 0 방향으로 내림합니다. 글은 제수가 컴파일 시점에 알려진 경우의 floor 나눗셈을 다루며, 이를 빠르게 계산하는 기존 알고리즘과 새로운 고속 기법을 소개합니다. 기법은 모든 비트 폭에서 쓸 수 있고 32비트나 SIMD 응용에도 도움이 되지만, 가장 큰 이점은 64비트에서 나타납니다. 또한 양수 나머지 연산과 유클리드 나눗셈을 더 빠르게 하는 데에도 활용할 수 있습니다. 벤치마크에서는 여러 플랫폼에서 제수별 처리량과 지연 시간을 비교합니다.

items.title: CNC Stone Carving
items.content:
In a form of architecture so ancient, CNC machines may seem a little out of place.  However, when one considers that the medieval builders were always on the forefront of the technology of their day, it no longer seems so strange.  To build Gothic today, it must become a reality, not a romantic idea locked up forever in one’s head.

(The Carmelite Monks spend their allotted work time on construction. See their Horarium here.)

CNC machines and robots have unlocked the ability to relatively quickly carve the intense details of a Gothic church.  Ornate pieces that used to take months for a skilled carver, now can be accomplished in a matter of days.  Instead of cutting out the beauty, using the excuse that it takes too long, thus doesn’t fit into the budget, modern technology can be used to make true Gothic in all its beauty a reality again today.

The use of modern technologies in stone carving unlock the potential of modern youth.  Though they may be untrained in the use of a hammer and chisel, young men and women have grown up in a world of computers.  The skills they possess can now be channeled towards a higher end, the building of a church for the glory of God.

CNC stands for “computer numerically controlled”, where a computer, through a series of XYZ coordinates, controls the movements of a machine.  The first CNC was invented for the manufacturing of airplane parts.  Stone cutting CNC machines are a relatively new invention.

Stone carving CNC machines typically use diamond tipped blades and milling bits, not water or laser, to carve the stone.  The diamonds, harder than the stone, grind away at the stone and wear it away.  The water is simply to keep the diamond tool from heating up from the friction and to wash away the stone sludge created by the carving process.

Normally the stone carving CNC machines used for sculptures and foliage have 5 axes, being able to move left and right, up and down, front and back, and rotate their heads in two different ways. The machines interpolate these multiple axes in order to carve the stone.  “Interpolate” means to work together, and an axis is one direction of motion.  So, the machines can move left, and down, and rotate their heads all at the same time to reach into a small area or leave a particular finish on the stone.    Sometimes they will even have a 6th axis, typically a lathe or a turntable, for carving tall stones such as pinnacles or statues.  The lathe interpolates with the other axes, carefully positioning itself to allow the CNC machine to reach each area of the stone.   CNC machines can also carve stone unattended, sometimes for long periods at a time and overnight.  This means 40 hours, a typical week of work, is less than 2 days for a CNC, a significant time savings!

The Carmelite Monks use CNC machines from Prussiani Engineering, a stone CNC manufacturer based out of Bergamo, Italy.  Italians have always been at the forefront of stone carving, and it is no different with modern technology.  With Prussiani’s machines the monks can carve levels of detail previously reserved to the hand carving of highly skilled craftsmen.  With the mindset “where there’s a will, there’s a way” and careful programming the machines’ capabilities are practically limitless and have the ability to carve unprecedented 3D reliefs.

items.title: Ghostty 1.4.0

Release notes for Ghostty 1.4.0, released on October 27, 2026.

Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release that includes large performance and

memory improvements, a 100% complete Kitty graphics implementation including

animation and relative placements (the first non-Kitty terminal to do so),

SSH integration improvements, and hundreds more improvements and fixes

This release features 7 months of work with changes from

172 contributors over 2,889 commits . Thank you to all the contributors,

maintainers, community moderators, translators, packagers, and users

who each helped make this release possible.

These release notes are painstakingly and lovingly hand-crafted

by human Ghostty maintainers, including the full changelog. They take

a combined 16+ hours to write, so please enjoy. 🥰

hasn't assigned them yet. If/when they're assigned, I will update the

Programs that display animated images with the Kitty protocol, such as an

control are all supported, and animations pause while the terminal isn't

visible. Relative placements let a program position one image relative to

another image's placement, so the child image moves along with its parent.

We also did a full conformance pass against the specification and Kitty

itself, fixing dozens of behavioral differences. For example, images now

scroll with text inside scroll regions ( #4323 ), retransmitting an image

ID replaces the old image ( #6711 ), and invalid image data now gets an

error response instead of silence, which could leave clients hanging. The

full list is in the terminal capabilities section.

Kitty graphics are faster, too. Image payloads are now parsed in bulk

with SIMD instead of one byte at a time, making large image transfers

about 16x faster to parse in our benchmarks (64 MiB of image data,

x86_64 Linux), and drawing images costs much less per frame.

Our Kitty graphics implementation now covers 100% of the published

specification, making Ghostty (and libghostty) the first terminal

PRs: #13264 #13473 #13240 #13245 #14130 #14137 #14138

Ghostty now transparently compresses scrollback that isn't visible,

reducing the physical memory those pages use by 70% to 90% for typical

text-heavy history. Compression only runs while the terminal is idle and

pages are decompressed on demand when you scroll back or search, so it

has no measurable impact on I/O throughput.

Thanks to compression, the default scrollback limit has been raised from

10 MB to 50 MB per terminal. On platforms that support compression, a

full scrollback still generally uses less physical memory than the old

Compression lowers resident (physical) memory, not virtual memory, so

look at resident memory when measuring it. It is currently available on

Beyond scrollback, memory usage is lower in many places:

items.content:
"If ten years ago the proposition of leading tech workers into collective action sounded preposterous in most of the world, today it is regarded not only as a possibility, but as a

necessity. Organized tech workers, given their position, are the one of the best point of leverage against the growing power of tech oligarchs. We believe in the potential for

change represented by workers who today waste their labor building dreadful and harmful technology.

The tech industry must be cleansed from within.

With this zine, we want to give space to the many people who have committed their time and their energy to fuel the Tech Workers Movement. While some of us make headlines every few months, the outside world still struggles to imagine what a tech labor organizer looks like, how they think, what they want, and why they do what they do.

Tech workers are not tech bros, and we want everybody to know."

This is the opening of Tendrils . Tendrils is TWC Global’s first zine, and it is launching today, after a pre-launch at the Circuit Breakers conference in NY and the Tech Workers Conference in Berlin.

We realized it’s time for tech workers to develop their own identity beyond their direct working conditions, an approach that proved complicated due to the complexity and fragmentation of the tech sector across the world. Commonality must be found beyond what our bosses take from us during working hours.

The result is a zine bringing together stories of tech workers from all over the world, using their skills for what they believe is Good and True. From sending money to Palestine, bypassing financial blockades, to building the infrastructure and the digital sovereignty of a mass movement in Brazil.

We invite you to read, print, circulate, and promote our zine in your local chapters and bring it to other tech workers’ spaces. If what you have read motivates you, we suggest you join Tech Workers Coalition to find your path through organizing in the End Times.

items.title: Conostigmus vitreus and Conostigmus obsidianus — two new parasitoid wasp species from Xizang, China
items.content:
Two Glassy and Obsidian-Like Parasitoid Wasp Species Discovered in Xizang, China

Two previously unknown species of parasitoid wasps have been formally described from the Xizang Autonomous Region of China, adding to the known diversity of a genus whose members are easy to overlook but ecologically significant. The new species, named Conostigmus vitreus and Conostigmus obsidianus, belong to the family Megaspilidae within the superfamily Ceraphronoidea, a group of small wasps that parasitize other insects. The description, published in the journal ZooKeys, is based on specimens collected in Xizang and preserved in the Insect Collection of Anhui Normal University in Wuhu, China. Alongside the morphological descriptions and illustrations, the authors generated DNA barcode sequences for both species and rebuilt a small phylogeny of the genus, providing molecular evidence that the two forms are distinct from each other and from previously described relatives.

Megaspilidae is a globally distributed family of small parasitoid wasps, occurring across all major biogeographic regions except Antarctica. Members of the family can be recognized by a suite of diagnostic features: a forewing with a well-developed large pterostigma, a curved radial sector crossvein in the forewing, two apical spurs on each tibia, and a mesoscutum that typically bears three longitudinal furrows, sometimes reduced. More than 450 valid species in 12 genera are currently recognized worldwide, and recent intensive revisions indicate that a large proportion of the family’s species diversity remains undescribed. The genus Conostigmus, established by Dahlbom in 1858 and initially treated as a subgenus of Megaspilus before being elevated to generic rank by Kieffer in 1907, is the most species-rich and widely distributed genus within the family, with approximately 190 valid described species and its highest diversity concentrated in the Palaearctic region.

China’s Conostigmus fauna has remained comparatively poorly documented. Only 17 species had been formally recorded from the country before this study, despite the genus’s strong Palaearctic diversity. Diagnostic characters for the genus include cylindrical male flagellomeres, a female first flagellomere less than 1.5 times as long as the pedicel, and an ocular ocellar length equal to or greater than the posterior ocellar length. One persistent complication in studying these wasps is that strong sexual dimorphism is widespread in Conostigmus, which often makes morphological association of conspecific males and females difficult or unreliable. For this reason, DNA barcode data, especially sequences of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene, have become increasingly important for confirming conspecificity and linking sexes in taxonomic work on the genus.

The specimens behind the new species were collected using sweep nets, Malaise traps, and yellow pan traps, and all were preserved in absolute ethanol immediately after collection. Specimen accession codes follow a standardized prefix system in which “XZMT-” denotes specimens collected from Medog (Motuo), Xizang, and “MXZ-” abbreviates Malaise trap collections from Xizang. For morphological imaging, specimens were air-dried and stabilized with molding clay, then photographed with a Leica M205A stereomicroscope equipped with a Leica DFC-500 digital camera; image stacking was processed with Leica Application Suite software and final plates edited in Adobe Photoshop. Male genitalia were dissected after macerating the apical metasomal segments in 35% hydrogen peroxide in a boiling water bath for five minutes, and stored in glycerin. All linear measurements are given in micrometers, except body length excluding antennae, which is given in millimeters.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-61575 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False AVideo is a video-sharing Platform. Prior to 8.1.0, `view/queue.php` uses `pathinfo` on the caller-controlled `fileURI` and stores its filename through `setTitle` in `encoder_queue.title` without neutralization. `fileURI` is not in the `objects/security.php` filter lists, and the `Login::canUpload()` capability needed to submit a queue entry can be self-granted using an attacker-controlled login site without legitimate encoder credentials. `view/index.php` loads `queue.json` from `view/queue.json.php` into the `#grid` jQuery Bootgrid table; its title formatter concatenates `row.title` into raw cell HTML. An attacker can therefore store an HTML title whose event handler runs in a privileged viewer's browser. `Encoder::getAll` limits nonadministrators to their own streamer's rows, so the victim must be an administrator who sees all rows or an operator on the attacker's streamer. A second `.html()` sink in the progress panel uses the same title but additionally depends on a helper script loaded from the streamer; the Bootgrid sink is reachable from encoder code alone. Billion-query-per-second lookup tables in C++
items.content:
A lot of software spends its time mapping strings to values. A web server must identify the HTTP method ( GET , POST , …). It must recognize header names. A URL parser must recognize the protocol ( http , https , ftp , …). A compiler must recognize keywords.

In C++, the default approach is to put the strings in a std::unordered_map .

std :: unordered_map < std :: string_view , Method > methods = {

{ "GET" , Method :: GET }, { "POST" , Method :: POST }, { "PUT" , Method :: PUT },

{ "DELETE" , Method :: DELETE }, { "PATCH" , Method :: PATCH }};

It works. But notice something: the keys are known when you write the code. They never change. And yet we pay at runtime as if they could change at any time: we hash the whole string, we pick a bucket, we follow a pointer, we compare, maybe we walk a list.

A hash function maps keys to slots. When two keys land in the same slot, we have a collision, and we must deal with it. Collisions are what make hash tables complicated and slow.

If you know all of your keys ahead of time, you can construct a hash function designed for your keys, a function that never produces a collision. It is called a perfect hash function. The idea is old: the GNU gperf tool has been doing it since 1989. You give it a list of keywords, and it generates C code.

We follow the same design as gperf . The slot for a key is computed as follows.

slot = ( length + asso [ key[i ]] + asso [ key[j ]] + ...) % table_size

We add the length of the key to a few small values taken from an association table ( asso ) indexed by the characters at a few selected positions. Usually, one or two positions are enough. The table size is a power of two, so the modulo is a single bitwise AND.

Consider the four HTTP methods GET , PUT , POST and DELETE . We use only the first character. Set asso['G'] = 0 , asso['P'] = 1 and asso['D'] = 0 . Then GET goes in slot 3 + 0 = 3, PUT goes in slot 3 + 1 = 4, POST goes in slot 4 + 1 = 5 and DELETE goes in slot 6 + 0 = 6. No collision.

To look up PUT , we compute the slot (4), and we compare PUT with the one key stored in slot 4. One hash, one comparison. If you look up PATCH , which is not in the set, you land in slot 5 + 1 = 6, you compare with DELETE , and you are done: not found. There is no probing, no chain to walk.

How do we find the association values? We sort the characters by how many keys they touch. We then take them one at a time and try 0, 1, 2, … until we find a value that does not cause a collision. We never revise a value once it is set. It is a greedy algorithm with bounded work. The bound matters because we do all of this at compile time, and C++ compilers limit how much work a constexpr function may do.

With our library , you write ordinary C++23. There is no external tool to run.

enum class Method { GET , POST , PUT , DELETE , PATCH };

constexpr auto methods = make_perfect_map <

The map is a compile-time constant. The compiler searches for the perfect hash function when it compiles your code. At runtime, computing the hash can take as few as four instructions: load one byte of the key, load one byte from the association table, add the length, apply a mask.

Computing the hash is cheap. But we still need to check that the string we are looking up matches the key stored in the slot. And comparing strings can be expensive: the textbook approach is a loop over the bytes with a branch for each byte. You can easily end up with dozens of instructions and several branches, and the branches are hard to predict when the strings vary.

Instead, we treat the key as a vector. Our processors, whether ARM or x64, have 16-byte registers. So we load 16 bytes unconditionally, even if the key is only three bytes long. We then use a shuffle instruction ( tbl on ARM NEON) to zero the bytes past the end of the key. The stored keys are zero-padded at compile time. A single vector comparison handles the whole key. We go from about forty instructions and eight branches to five instructions…

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Instagram is testing 90-minute videos
items.content:
Credit: Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Instagram is introducing longform video. Called Features, the new format will allow users to upload videos up to 90 minutes long.

Instagram will now edit the first draft of your Reel for you

"So many creators are producing longer videos, and they're using clips of those videos to drive discovery on Reels and help build their audience," said Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons , announcing Features in a video alongside Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri on Monday.

"Reels is still going to be a core part of Instagram. But when you want to go deeper with creators you love and the content they're creating, you should be able to do that on Instagram."

Longform video creators have typically favoured YouTube, which allows verified accounts to upload videos up to 12 hours long . In contrast, Instagram Reels are restricted to a maximum length of 20 minutes . Features aims to allow these creators to share their longer videos on Instagram as well, keeping their audience on the platform.

Features appears to focus on content shot in landscape, and will be available on desktop, the mobile app, and Instagram for TV . Lyons stated that part of the new format's purpose is to help populate Instagram's television app, which allows users to watch Reels and video content on their TV.

Sign up for Mashable's weekly Light Speed newsletter.

By clicking Sign Me Up, you confirm you are 16+ and agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .

"We've been working on a TV version of Reels, and we know that to do that well, we need more than just short-form video," said Lyons.

"People might discover a long form video that they love by seeing a Reel that's a clip of the video when they're watching Reels on mobile, and then when they go at the end of the day and open their TV and open Instagram on TV, we'll know that they watched that Reel and we'll be able to say, 'Hey, do you want to finish watching…?'"

Though Instagram is introducing longform functionality, it doesn't yet offer creators the same financial incentives as YouTube. While Instagram creators are primarily paid through third-party brand partnerships and collaborations , the YouTube Partner Program gives YouTubers a cut of revenue from ads placed on their videos (55 percent for longform and 45 percent for Shorts).

At time of writing, the most liked comment on Mosseri and Lyons' post was from mental health content creator Divija Bhasin ( @awkwardgoat3 ), who asked, "Why would anyone post an unpaid long video on Instagram if we can just post it on YouTube and actually get paid for the effort?"

"Over time, we think there will be compounding benefits for creators to tell new stories, reach new audiences, and find new partners, which should lead to many monetization opportunities," the Instagram spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Prior to 8.1.0, the unauthenticated streamer login at `objects/login.json.php` passes the `user` parameter to `Streamer::get` in `objects/Streamer.php`, where it is interpolated into a single-quoted MariaDB SELECT without parameterization or escaping. Although `objects/security.php` strips literal single quotes, `html_entity_decode` in `objects/Login.php` restores entity-encoded quotes before the query. The supplied `siteURL` must pass the streamer allowlist, which allows all sites when empty by default, and an attacker-hosted login response must set `canUpload` or `isAdmin` to reach `Streamer::createIfNotExists`. That function calls `Streamer::get` before its additional allowlist check. UNION results are exposed through `streamers_id`, while failures return the rendered query and MariaDB error. An attacker can read arbitrary encoder database data, including stored upstream streamer credentials, allowlist configuration, and queue records, without encoder credentials. Stacked statements are not permitted by the mysqli driver and the tested database account lacks global FILE privilege, so the demonstrated vector is bounded to reads rather than server-side file writes. Stolen streamer credentials can provide continued upstream access until rotated. This issue is fixed in version 8.1.0. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-28T21:54:38.358Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-61569
